summary: The article reports on growing efforts to embed art education in school curricula through educator voices, advocacy campaigns, and community partnerships. It profiles Samantha Holt, Gregory Chan's Creative Integration Project, Elaine Morris's 'Every Child Deserves Art' campaign, and a Roosevelt Middle School partnership with the Contemporary Art Center of Middleton. Student stories from Maria Alvarez and Jamal Carter illustrate the impact of arts on engagement and community.
one_line: Educators, advocates, and community partners are working to integrate art across school curricula, with student success stories showing benefits for engagement and community.
key_facts: Samantha Holt, an art educator at Lincoln Elementary, was interviewed on September 15, 2023, and said "Art is not just about making things look pretty."
Holt contrasts math and science, where answers are often black or white, with the art room, where "the spectrum of possibility is endless."
The 'Creative Integration Project' launched on October 3, 2023, created by local art advocates, educators like Holt, and the city council's cultural department.

Gregory Chan, a project leader of the Creative Integration Project, was met at Jackson High School's art studio; he aims to weave art into all school subjects, e.g., fresco painting workshops in Renaissance history lessons or kinetic sculptures in physics.
Elaine Morris founded the 'Every Child Deserves Art' campaign and spoke at a rally on November 10, 2023, saying quality art education is "a right, not a privilege."
The 'Every Child Deserves Art' campaign engages stakeholders from policymakers to parents and has led to policy discussions and increased funding for art education in several school districts.
Roosevelt Middle School and the Contemporary Art Center of Middleton began a partnership on December 1, 2023.
Principal Laura Gibson called the Roosevelt-Middleton partnership "a symbiotic relationship" in which students gain exposure to cutting-edge art and artists get a platform to inspire.
Center Director Michael Trevino said students give artists fresh perspectives through their unfiltered view of the world.
Maria Alvarez, a 10th grader at Jefferson High, found pottery in art class after being disengaged, leading to improved attendance and performance.
Jamal Carter, a 7th grader, took part in a school mural project inspired by local history and said "This is our mark."
Community partnerships include local artists volunteering time, galleries opening to students, and businesses sponsoring supplies and initiatives.
